newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open higher after bargain-hunting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open higher after bargain-hunting.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Monday in line with modest overseas gains.

Analysts said bargain-hunting helped to give prices a firmer tone overnight, but gains were capped by market concerns that the July U.S. retail sales report, due on Wednesday, would show that consumer spending was picking up after tapering off in the second quarter.
At 0800 EDT/1200 GMT, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 8/32 to 96-28/32, yielding 6.62 percent. Two-year notes were up 2/32 to 99-26/32, yielding 5.98 percent.

"We saw a little bit of bargain hunting and short-covering overnight, which given the debacle on Friday, is not a big surprise," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at Standard & Poor's MMS. "But really, the upside is still very limited."
Rupert said the market is waiting for the data on July retail sales, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Wednesday.
"The market fears the potential strength in the report that would suggest a fairly healthy rebound in spending activity after the lull in the second quarter," she said.
MMS and other economists polled by Reuters expect a 0.7 percent gain in July retail sales overall.
MMS anticipates a sales gain of 0.4 percent when auto transactions are excluded.
Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, a 0.5 percent sales gain, ex-autos.

Rupert characterized gains of that nature as "pretty solid gains" that would generate concern that third quarter economic activity would come in quite a bit stronger than second quarter activity and would eventually force the Federal Reserve to make monetary policy more restrictive.
Rupert said the markt would have to work to stay in the plus column on Monday.
"There will be some corrective activity (from last week's declines) but you will see people trying to sell on the upticks as well," she said.
Rupert located support for the cash 30-year bond at 96-13/32 and near 96-6/32 below that.

"The market was firmer overnight," said James Blumenthal, economist at MCM Moneywatch. "You had some correction from Friday's drop and you had some bargain-hunting coming in. It started in Tokyo and continued in London and that's basically what you're seeing here," he said.
With no data due on Monday, the market is "really waiting until Wednesday," when the government will release the July retail sales report, Blumenthal said.

"The tone will be cautious going into that," he said. "The real key to this week come later -- particularly the retail sales data and also the PPI (Producer Price Index) and CPI (Consumer Price Index) numbers."
Blumenthal said that after Friday's sharp decline, the market is "especially nervous" as it approaches those numbers and "feels vulnerable."
As a result, the market could see some consolidation after Friday's drop, Blumenthal said, "but it's going to be limited in front of those numbers."

At the short end of the maturity range, three- and six-month bill rates were each down one basis point to 5.14 percent and 5.22 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were down two basis points to 5.27 percent.

Two-year Treasury notes were up 1/32 to 99-25/32, yielding 5.99 percent. Five-year notes were up 2/32 to 99-4/32, yielding 6.21 percent. Ten-year notes were up 4/32 to 98-11/32, yielding 6.35 percent.
((-- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
